newsitem.title: USA: Green thumbs go online for supplies, advice.
newsitem.headline: Green thumbs go online for supplies, advice.

text.p: The earthly pursuits of gardening are not often associated with the high-tech of cyberspace, but Garden Escape hopes to change all that.
Green thumbs can order their gardening supplies, get planting advice and even plan their gardens on the Garden Escape web site.
"We're very much a gardening company that hopes to be one of the largest brands, rather than solely an Internet company," said Cliff Sharples, president and chief executive officer.
At the firm's World Wide Web site (www.garden.com), software can be downloaded for designing a garden using Garden Escape's products.
Sharples said the web site, which was created in March 1996, offers 10,000 different products, with the orders sent directly to nurseries and manufacturers for them to handle the shipping.

Regarding the price of his products, Sharples said, "We're not going to be the cheapest store in town, but we're not going to be too expensive. We've selected the highest quality suppliers and they are not necessarily the largest brands.
"Kmart and Home Depot will have lower prices, but they won't have our variety," he added.
So far, Sharples said, 100,000 people are currently members who have signed up to receive a free monthly newsletter and the website gets 6,000 visitors a day.
Sharples said gardening is very popular with Baby Boomers, which gives Garden Escape a lot of marketing opportunities.
Bruce Butterfield, director of research at the National Gardening Association, said people over 50 buy about half of the $22.5 billion of lawn and garden supplies sold in United States.

"It's clear that people are spending more time at home these days," Butterfield said about gardening's popularity. He cited gardening's affordability, the value it can add to a home and enjoyment of outdoors behind its popularity.
These demographics help Garden Escape to enter ventures with other retailers, such as a recent sweepstakes it had with Spiegel Inc.'s Eddie Bauer stores.
"That's the case with a lot of retailers -- to figure how the electronic marketplace could work in their strategy," Sharples said, noting that Spiegel has a good Internet presence.
Doug Berger, spokesman for Direct Marketing Association, said Internet retail figures vary widely, but the most common estimate for online sales is $500 million to $600 million.
The electronic marketplace is becoming kinder to Garden Escape with the web site generating 40 percent month-over-month sales growth since January, Sharples said.
He would not disclose sales figures, but he expects Garden Escape to be profitable by early 1999.
Garden Escape just raised $5.25 million of its total $8 million in venture capital in a new round of financing, which included investors such as Scripps Ventures, a unit of E.W. Scripps.
Scripps also owns Home & Garden Television, a cable television channel.
Sharples would not rule out a future venture with the cable television channel, "but it is not necessarily a given that we would do something on Home Garden Television."
"We've been focused on building the technology and content, building team and arranging supply partners," Sharples said.
"This spring we started actively marketing the site. We don't want to give a customer a bad experience, we want to manage our growth," Sharples said.
So even in the world of cyberspace, the rules of retailing still apply.
